newsitem.title: CONGO: Fighting dies down in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fighting dies down in Brazzaville.

text.p: Fighting died down in Congo's capital Brazzaville on Thursday as a ceasefire appeared to be holding after a week of fierce clashes between forces loyal to the president and a former Marxist military ruler.
Only occasional shots could be heard in the city centre wrecked by the fighting between President Pascal Lissouba's troops and the Cobra militia of Denis Sassou Nguesso before Wednesday's ceasefire.
"It's much more calm today than it has been before. Really there is nothing happening," French military spokesman Captain Alexis Jaraud told Reuters.
Earlier on Thursday, mortar blasts and grenade explosions echoed around some areas near the Brazzaville airport after sporadic shooting overnight.
In the city centre, the body of a boy of about eight lay on the roadside in an area controlled by Sassou Nguesso's forces -- with a gunshot in the head and his school bag still on his back.
Other corpses lay in other streets, but no overall death toll was available because aid worker and military officials had not reached all areas of fighting.
Many shops were looted and several buildings were burned down.
"We obey the order to stop firing," Sombi Anisse, a Cobra fighter, told Reuters. "The others started firing around five o'clock. We haven't responded and it has been calm here."
But another Cobra soldier, Eyenga Simplice, said his comrades had no intention of sticking to the ceasefire and wanted to seize power.
The front-line runs roughly along Avenue de la Paix (Peace), one of the capital's major thoroughfares.
Clashes erupted last week after government troops surrounded the home of Sassou Nguesso in a crackdown on militias ahead of a July 27 presidential election.
Lissouba said on state radio on Wednesday: "I order an immediate ceasefire to give a chance for mediation. Peace must remain our first objective."

Hours later, Sassou Nguesso said on his militia's own radio station, Radio Congo Freedom: "I ask that the arms be silent and hope that other parties, at least this time, respect their commitments, and that the parties in conflict will keep their positions on the ground."
France, the former colonial power, said on Wednesday its armed forces had evacuated 1,778 foreigners, two-thirds of them French nationals, to nearby Gabon by air since Monday.
United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday called for a halt to the fighting in Brazzaville.

"The secretary-general is increasingly concerned about the deteriorating situation in Congo Brazzaville and the rising human toll in this conflict," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said in a statement. "He calls on the parties to cease hostilities and promptly begin negotiations to settle their differences."

In a clear sign that Washington believed Sassou Nguesso was in the wrong, the State Department on Wednesday said it deeply regretted that "rebel groups, opposition groups, have decided to take their fight to the streets".
Spokesman Nicholas Burns urged Sassou Nguesso to agree to international mediation.

Lissouba's ceasefire call followed a meeting on Tuesday with Brazzaville Mayor Bernard Kolelas, who is chairing a mediation committee of the two sides. A spokesman for Kolelas said that he had spoken by telephone on Wednesday with Sassou Nguesso.

Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics. Lissouba defeated Kolelas in the second round after Sassou Nguesso was knocked out in the first round.
Kolelas's Ninja militia was at the heart of similar fighting which killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994, but it has kept out of the latest fighting.
